strengths: Addresses a practical and important problem (real-time streaming infinite-length avatar generation) with strong experimental validation across multiple benchmarks and metrics
Comprehensive technical framework thoughtfully combining multiple mechanisms (TPP, RSFM, History Corrupt, AAS) to solve interconnected challenges of latency and long-horizon consistency
Strong empirical results with competitive or superior performance on GenBench and AVSpeech, validated by extensive ablations (Tables 3-4, 7) and user study confirming perceptual alignment
Achieves practical 20 FPS streaming performance on 5 H800 GPUs with detailed runtime analysis and efficiency characterization
Extensive supplementary material with algorithms, extended experiments to 10,000 seconds, cross-dataset validation, and architectural justification
Well-motivated design choices (block-wise causal masking, rolling sink frame mechanism, adaptive attention sink) specifically tailored to streaming avatar generation
weaknesses: Limited fundamental algorithmic novelty - primarily combines existing techniques (diffusion models, SFDM from prior work, temporal adaptation) rather than introducing new algorithms or theory
Incomplete baseline comparisons missing direct evaluation against StreamDiff and LongLive; limited methods in AVSpeech benchmark; no computational cost comparison with baselines
Significant domain gap in evaluation - training only on 5-second clips with inference extrapolating to 10,000+ seconds (200× extrapolation) lacks rigorous justification of generalization capability

Technical clarity issues including sparse explanation of block-wise noise scheduling, incomplete specification of training convergence criteria, and important insights (History Corrupt effectiveness) relegated to appendix
User study limited in scope (20 participants, 30 videos) for supporting claims about human perception; custom OOD evaluation limited to GenBench dataset without external validation
Reproducibility concerns including unspecified hyperparameters (loss weights, learning rates per training stage), unavailable code, and challenging dataset acquisition
High computational requirements (5 H800 GPUs for 20 FPS) with no analysis of scaling properties; TPP framework complexity may limit adoption
Evaluation metrics including custom Sync-C/Sync-D lack detailed methodology in main text and comparison with standard audio-visual synchronization metrics from literature

strengths: Addresses genuine practical challenges in real-time video generation with solid engineering: the Timestep-forcing Pipeline Parallelism effectively enables distributed inference across GPUs without inter-GPU communication bottlenecks, achieving 20 FPS on large models—a real deployment achievement.

Comprehensive experimental validation with multiple baselines (Ditto, Echomimic-V2, HalloL3, StableAvatar, OmniAvatar, WanS2V), ablation studies demonstrating impact of each component, long-horizon generation tests (10,000 seconds), and human user study providing multi-faceted evidence.
Demonstrates consistent quality improvements across multiple standard metrics (ASE, IQA, Sync-CT, Sync-DI, Dino-S) and achieves better human preference scores, showing the system works in practice.
Technical presentation is complete with detailed algorithms, pseudocode, implementation details, and supplementary material, supporting reproducibility and understanding.
Includes thoughtful ethical discussion (Section 13) addressing privacy, consent, and responsible deployment—important for avatar generation technology.
weaknesses: Limited fundamental novelty: core contributions are engineering applications of existing techniques. Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) is from prior work [31]; Self-Forcing builds on [19]; Timestep-forcing is straightforward distributed execution; Rolling cache mechanisms apply standard techniques. Combinations are sensible but not methodologically novel.

Lacks theoretical foundation: no formal analysis of why the Rolling Sink Frame Mechanism addresses identity drift better than alternatives, no temporal consistency bounds, no principled justification for design choices like block-wise noise scheduling or History Corrupt strategy.

Overstated claims: 'infinite length' generation is actually bounded at 10,000 seconds; 'state-of-the-art' comparisons lack rigor (baselines from different time periods, potentially different training conditions); some metric improvements are modest.

Evaluation limitations: user study limited to 20 participants; metrics (ASE, IQA) have known limitations for avatar assessment; GenBench is synthetic and limited; missing analysis of failure cases, failure modes, or explicit discussion of when the approach breaks down (briefly mentioned for TPP but not elaborated).

Incomplete technical justification: base model training details insufficiently specified; hyperparameter choices lack justification; text conditioning appears to be frame reference injection rather than true multimodal modeling; no explanation for why these specific design choices outperform alternatives.

Reproducibility concerns: code availability unclear; critical details in supplementary material; generalization to diverse real-world avatars/scenarios not thoroughly tested beyond synthetic GenBench.

Presentation density: core contributions somewhat buried in implementation details; key insights could be clearer; paper reads as detailed engineering documentation rather than a research contribution with clear conceptual advances.

Reframed as Systems/Applications work, the paper's low novelty becomes more apparent: it's highly competent engineering combining known techniques but lacks the methodological or conceptual contribution expected at a top-tier vision conference.

strengths: Addresses two important but previously unaddressed challenges simultaneously: real-time inference latency and long-horizon consistency in audio-driven avatar generation

Comprehensive experimental validation with 8+ state-of-the-art baselines, extensive ablation studies (Tables 3, 4, 7), and user study (20 participants) confirming superiority across visual quality, synchronization, and naturalness metrics
Impressive practical achievement: achieves 20.88 FPS with a 14B-parameter model on 5 H800 GPUs while maintaining competitive visual quality (ASE=3.38, IQA=4.73 on long video)
Novel distributed inference paradigm (TPP) that cleverly parallelizes the sequential diffusion chain without inter-GPU communication bottlenecks, enabling genuine real-time streaming
Rigorous long-horizon evaluation up to 10,000 seconds demonstrates stability and consistency that existing methods cannot achieve, with detailed metrics showing no quality degradation
Well-designed mechanisms (RSFM and AAS) effectively address identity drift and color artifacts, with ablation clearly demonstrating their necessity
Complete technical documentation: detailed algorithms (1-4), comprehensive hyperparameters, implementation specifics, and extensive supplementary materials (13 sections)
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (Figures 2-3, 6-9) that clearly communicate the framework, pipeline parallelism, and qualitative comparisons
Thoughtful discussion of ethical considerations (Section 13) addressing privacy, consent, and misuse concerns
Strong practical impact with clear potential for real-world deployment in telepresence, virtual assistants, and interactive applications
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Diffusion Forcing is from prior work [3], and Distribution Matching Distillation from [19]. The paper primarily combines existing techniques rather than introducing fundamentally new concepts, limiting conceptual contribution

TPP scalability analysis is incomplete: requires T GPUs for T diffusion steps, which becomes prohibitively expensive for models with many steps. The 4-step compressed model may represent a significant quality-complexity tradeoff not thoroughly analyzed

Insufficient analysis of distillation trade-offs: the paper doesn't quantify quality loss from reducing from higher-step models to 4 steps, making it unclear what performance ceiling was sacrificed for efficiency

RSFM and AAS mechanisms, while effective, are relatively ad-hoc solutions: lack principled theoretical justification for why rolling sink frames specifically prevent identity drift, and history corruption strategy appears empirically motivated rather than grounded in theory

Dataset generalization concerns: evaluation primarily on talking-face generation with proprietary synthetic GenBench dataset. Unclear how well the method generalizes to non-human avatars or diverse character types
User study scale is modest (20 participants) and custom metrics (Sync-C) lack standardization, limiting comparison with potential future work and community adoption
Limited failure case analysis: no discussion of when the method struggles, under what audio characteristics it degrades, or how performance evolves beyond the tested 10,000s horizon

Reproducibility gaps: exact distillation procedure from higher-step models not detailed, training computational cost unspecified, and reliance on WanS2V pretraining creates dependency on external models
TPP requires multiple synchronized GPUs, limiting practical accessibility for researchers/practitioners with limited hardware resources

Incomplete ablation on design choices: no exploration of alternative KV-cache strategies, different rollout window sizes, or sensitivity analysis for key hyperparameters (e.g., cache length, block size)

strengths: Achieves first practical real-time streaming of 14B diffusion model for infinite-length avatar generation at 45 FPS with 1.21s TTFF on 5 H800 GPUs - a significant engineering accomplishment

Well-designed system combining complementary technical strategies: two-stage training (diffusion forcing + self-forcing), three long-horizon stability mechanisms (History Corrupt, Adaptive Attention Sink, Rolling RoPE), and system-level Timestep-forcing Pipeline Parallelism

Comprehensive experimental validation with extensive ablations (Tables 3-6), long-horizon evaluation to 10,000+ seconds, multiple metrics (ASE, IQA, audio-visual sync, identity consistency), user study with perceptual evaluation, and comparisons against 6 state-of-the-art baselines
Introduces GenBench benchmark for long-form avatar video evaluation exceeding 5 minutes, enabling reproducible evaluation and supporting future research

Solid technical soundness with proper justification of design choices through ablations, detailed pseudocode for reproducibility (Algorithms 1-4), and commitment to release code and evaluation scripts
Clear presentation with effective technical diagrams explaining architecture (Figs. 2, 9-10) and inference procedures, making complex system design accessible
Addresses ethical considerations including privacy, consent, and responsible deployment guidelines for audio-driven avatar generation
weaknesses: Limited fundamental algorithmic novelty - individual components (History Corrupt heuristic, Adaptive Attention Sink adaptation, Rolling RoPE modification, TPP parallelization) are incremental adaptations of known techniques; novelty primarily in system combination rather than novel algorithms

Training-test distribution mismatch: model trained on 5-second clips but evaluated at 10,000 seconds; while impressive, this extrapolation beyond training distribution deserves deeper analysis of why stable generation persists

Evaluation specialized to talking-head scenarios on GenBench; generalization to diverse avatar types (full-body, stylized, non-human characters) and other domains not explored, limiting generalizability claims

Incomplete technical justifications: History Corrupt pattern choice lacks ablation, RoPE offset range (~40k) not principled, why three distinct strategies are necessary insufficiently explained beyond empirical evidence

Scalability concerns: evaluation uses single 14B architecture; generalization to different model sizes/architectures unclear; single-GPU throughput substantially lower, limiting practical accessibility despite claiming real-time capability
Hardware dependency: requires 5 H800 GPUs for 45 FPS; cloud deployment costs and single-GPU performance implications not discussed; limits reproducibility and practical deployment

Overstated claims about 'infinite length' despite practical limits under specific conditions (static-scene priors, training on 5s clips); interaction latency requirements for bidirectional telepresence not discussed
Missing efficiency analysis: no energy consumption, carbon footprint, or cost comparison for cloud deployment; memory requirements and scalability with fewer GPUs not thoroughly explored

Audio conditioning limited to English-centric dataset (AVSpeech); sensitivity to audio quality/encoding and cross-language generalization not explored despite audio being central to driving avatar motion

Metric limitations: audio-visual synchronization metrics (Sync-C/D) rely on pre-trained models that may not perfectly capture human perception; broader perceptual evaluation beyond user study would strengthen claims

strengths: Addresses an important and practically relevant problem of real-time, streaming, infinite-length audio-driven avatar generation
Complete system design spanning both training (two-stage framework) and inference (TPP parallelism) components
Achieves impressive practical results: 45.2 FPS with 1.21s TTFF on 5 H800 GPUs, competitive with or exceeding baselines on multiple metrics

Comprehensive experimental evaluation with extensive ablations (Tables 3-6), long-horizon extrapolation study (Table 7), user study (Table 9), and detailed supplementary materials including pseudocode
Well-motivated design rationale for three long-horizon stability strategies with clear explanation of different failure modes they address
Introduces GenBench, a standardized long-term video generation benchmark with multiple evaluation subsets and out-of-domain testing
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: individually borrowed components (Self-Forcing [18], DMD [52], motion frames) without significant innovation; proposed stabilization strategies (History Corrupt, AAS, Rolling RoPE) lack theoretical justification and appear as empirical heuristics

Insufficient ablation clarity: Table 4 doesn't cleanly isolate individual contributions of the three long-horizon strategies; no principled justification for design choices (e.g., why noisy KV cache vs. other regularization methods)

Evaluation limitations: metrics dependent on face alignment may not generalize to extreme extrapolation; artificial audio-looping setup for 10,000s test; user study limited to 20 participants; limited comparison with recent end-to-end video generation methods
Severe hardware requirements (5×H800 GPUs) significantly limit practical applicability and reproducibility; no results on more accessible hardware configurations
Narrow scope: evaluation limited to talking head videos (AVSpeech) and synthetic data (GenBench); unclear generalization to body motion, complex gestures, or diverse avatar models

Presentation issues: concepts introduced informally (History Corrupt naming unclear), Figure 2 difficult to parse, dense writing, key details relegated to appendix; paper length (33 pages) could be condensed
No discussion of failure cases, degradation patterns, or boundary conditions for long-horizon generation stability; missing sensitivity analysis for hyperparameters
TPP parallelism lacks novelty—essentially standard pipelining with each GPU processing one timestep; speedup gains are engineering-focused rather than algorithmic
Reproducibility concerns: scattered hyperparameter specifications, code unavailable, some design decisions unclear without detailed appendix review

strengths: Tackles a genuinely challenging and practically important problem combining streaming, real-time inference, and infinite-length generation at 14B scale
Comprehensive two-stage training framework with well-motivated complementary strategies (History Corrupt, AAS, Rolling RoPE) addressing specific failure modes
Impressive empirical results: 45 FPS with 1.21s TTFF, outperforms baselines across multiple metrics, maintains quality at 10,000+ seconds—unprecedented for diffusion avatars
Thorough experimental rigor with extensive ablations (Tables 3-6), user study with 20 participants, and reproducibility details enabling community validation
TPP (Timestep-forcing Pipeline Parallelism) is a creative engineering contribution solving sequential bottlenecks in diffusion sampling
GenBench benchmark with diverse characters and long-duration videos will benefit future research; clear commitment to release data and code
Includes ethical considerations for responsible deployment of avatar generation systems
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: History Corrupt, AAS, and Rolling RoPE are incremental optimizations; Self-Forcing and DMD are existing techniques—contributions are primarily engineering-focused rather than introducing fundamentally new algorithms or theory

Overstated 'Infinite Length' claim: Table 7 shows measurable quality drift over 10,000 seconds (Dino-S 0.96→0.95); extrapolation is bound by RoPE positional divergence and 5-second motion-frame context window

Incomplete baseline comparisons: Missing direct comparison with LongLive [50] (also addresses long-form streaming); most baselines use smaller models; WanS2V (2025) is very recent; no cross-domain or few-GPU scaling studies

Lack of theoretical justification for long-horizon capability: Why these specific strategies enable extrapolation is not analyzed; KV cache noise scheduling appears ad-hoc without principled design justification

Narrow scope and generalization concerns: Evaluated only on talking-head avatars from AVSpeech; no cross-domain experiments or evaluation on different avatar types—avatar-specific design choices may not transfer

High computational cost limits deployment: Requires 8 H800 GPUs; end-to-end latency including network transmission for actual streaming scenarios not analyzed; TTFF of 1.21s may not meet interactive requirements

Audio-visual synchronization analysis: Sync metrics depend on ground-truth videos; validity unclear for extreme extrapolation; limited study of failure modes at 10,000+ seconds; minor flicker (T.Flicker 0.97) suggests some instability
Limited justification for design choices: Why 5-second motion frames are optimal, why specific noise schedules work best (Table 6), why block size 3 is default (Table 10 shows marginal differences)
